One resonant plant, one fixed drive-power budget, and every excitation you might reach for:
the **Fisher-optimal multisine**, a naive **cophased** multisine, a **swept sine**, and
**broadband and shaped noise**. Pick any of them and watch two numbers — and the whole
scoreboard — update live, all in your browser, no install.

## The two axes

Every drive here spends the **same total power**. What changes is *how* it spends it, and that
splits cleanly into two independent stories:

- **Time to identify to 5%** — set by the drive's **power spectrum** $P_{xx}(f)$ alone. This is
  the real Cramér–Rao bound (the same Fisher kernel as the [landing-page game](index.qmd) and the
  [`system_ident` pipeline](examples/interactive.qmd)). Pile power where the plant's modal
  parameters are least certain and the clock plummets; spread it flat and you wait ~40× longer.
  Notice that *every* flat-spectrum drive — flat multisine, white noise, a linear sweep — shares
  the **same** time, whatever its phase. Fisher can't tell them apart.

- **Crest factor** — how peaky the drive is, `max|x|/rms`. It matters because the actuator's DAC has
  a fixed range: a peaky drive clips (or forces you to turn the whole thing down, throwing away SNR).
  The **Fisher-optimal drive is naturally gentle** — it collapses onto ~2 tones, so its crest is ~2
  with nothing to tune. A **swept sine** is gentlest of all (~$\sqrt2$, a constant-envelope sine);
  broadband **noise** sits ~3.4; and a naively **cophased** multisine detonates into an impulse (~15)
  that would clip instantly. So the lever for headroom is the same as for speed — *concentrate the
  spectrum* — not any phase cleverness (see the caveat below).

## Why the optimal spectrum wins

The champion (★) is the **Fisher-optimal spectrum**. It collapses almost entirely onto **two tones**
(all the budget sits on the two resonances — effective line count ≈ 2), and that one fact buys both
prizes: it identifies the plant ~40× faster than any flat drive, *and* two tones are intrinsically
low-crest (~2), so it stays inside the actuator range for free. A swept sine matches that crest but
wastes power off-resonance; broadband noise loses on speed (and pays a further leakage / variance
penalty for being aperiodic). That is the case for
[optimal excitation](tutorial/why-optimal-excitation.qmd) — something you can *feel* by clicking,
before a single equation.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## A caveat on crest, and on phase tricks
Crest is the quantity the **DAC** sees, and this page measures it on the raw synthesized samples.
In a real actuator the drive is shaped by the whitening / actuation chain on its way to the DAC,
which reassigns the per-frequency phases — so a crest carefully minimized at synthesis (e.g. by a
Schroeder phase schedule) does **not** survive to where the range limit actually bites. The
dependable way to keep the drive within range is to keep its spectrum concentrated, which the
optimal design does anyway; phase-shaping is not a lever you can bank on here.
:::
